messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marta Holloway is a 26-year-old single woman of European descent who works as a firefighter in a mid-sized municipal department. She presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after being held captive for nearly four days following a structural collapse during a warehouse fire. While conducting an interior search with her crew, a secondary explosion brought down a section of the ceiling, separating Marta from her team and trapping her in a small debris pocket with a civilian victim who did not survive. She was conscious throughout, pinned in near-total darkness, subjected to intermittent sounds of the structure continuing to shift around her, and unable to move or call for help effectively. When she was finally located and extracted, she had sustained moderate physical injuries, but it was the psychological aftermath that proved most enduring.

In the weeks following her rescue, Marta noticed that certain things seemed to reach directly into the experience and pull it forward. Old photographs — particularly ones taken at the station or with her crew from before the incident — would bring the memory rushing back with a sudden, unwilled force, as though it had been waiting just behind the image. Crowded spaces carried a similar charge; the press of bodies and noise in a grocery store or a busy street corner would activate the memory with the same abruptness, stripping away the present and replacing it with the debris pocket. When these triggers fired, they did not merely remind her of what had happened — they seemed to confirm her worst beliefs about herself. She had come to believe, with quiet but absolute conviction, that she had caused what happened through her own poor judgment — that a different, more capable firefighter would have read the structure correctly and avoided the collapse. Each time a trigger pulled the memory forward, this self-blame reasserted itself, hardening a little more.

The memory itself had an unusual quality that Marta found deeply unsettling. It did not feel like ordinary recollection. It felt photographic — she could close her eyes and see the grain of the concrete beside her face, the angle of a fallen beam, with a precision that no ordinary memory had ever possessed. At the same time, it felt alien, as though it had happened to someone else, a dissociation that confused and frightened her. These qualities fed back into her self-appraisals: if the memory was this vivid, this insistent, this strange, surely it meant she was fundamentally broken. And the more she turned that belief over, the more readily the memory surfaced — the appraisals seemed to keep it close, to rehearse it, so that it required less and less prompting to arrive.

The threat state that had settled over Marta's daily life was pervasive. She startled violently at ordinary sounds — a door slamming in the firehouse, a car backfiring outside — and could not return to baseline quickly. Even when she understood intellectually that she was safe, her body refused the information; she was unable to relax in any sustained way, and the hyperarousal itself seemed to confirm her belief that she could no longer cope, that the smallest disturbance was now too much for her. In this heightened state, flashbacks arrived with particular force — sudden, full-sensory episodes in which she was back in the debris pocket, and the present vanished entirely. The threat state also kept her sensitised to triggers: crowded spaces, which she had once moved through without difficulty, now registered as threatening environments to be avoided, and the firehouse photographs that lined the common room walls had become objects she could not look at directly.

The loop had tightened considerably by the time Marta sought help. She had begun requesting administrative assignments to avoid active call responses, a change her supervisors had noticed and which she experienced as further evidence that she was no longer herself — that the person who had chosen this work and been good at it was gone. What finally brought her in was a shift in which she froze briefly during a routine drill, something that had never happened before. She arrived at the intake session quiet and precise in her self-report, but what she was most afraid of was that the self-blame was correct — that she had always been this fragile, and the collapse had simply revealed it. What she hoped, though she stated it carefully, was that she might one day feel like herself again.
